svg.text: The 2012 ingredient list, re-sorted by what happened next
The paper orders Sections 3.1 to 3.4 by its own estimate of importance. Fourteen years later only the first of the four survives.
SURVIVED — and why it stayed
ReLU and its descendants
Rectifiers are the default. The 2012 argument was wall-clock;
what kept them is gradient flow through depth.
Dropout
Still in transformer blocks and classifier heads. In vision it has
been pushed aside by stronger augmentation and normalisation.
Aggressive data augmentation
Crops, flips and colour jitter are table stakes, and the modern
recipes are far more aggressive than the two schemes here.
Betting on GPUs
The most durable sentence in the paper: results can be improved
simply by waiting for faster GPUs and bigger datasets.
End-to-end supervised depth
No unsupervised pre-training, no hand-designed features. Removing
any middle layer cost about 2% top-1 — depth was the point.
DID NOT SURVIVE — and what replaced it
Local response normalization
The reported 1.4% top-1 gain did not reproduce in VGG. Later
normalisation layers (batch, layer norm) replaced it.
The hand-split two-GPU topology
A 3 GB memory workaround, not a design. The follow-up work drops
it for data and model parallelism chosen per layer type.
Overlapping pooling, as a design lever
Worth 0.4% top-1 in 2012. Strided convolutions and global average
pooling took over; one 3×3/2 max-pool lingers in some stems.
Hand-driven learning-rate steps
Divide the rate by 10 whenever validation error stalls, manually,
three times. Replaced by warmup plus a schedule fixed in advance.
Ten-crop test-time averaging
Worth more than a point of top-1 here, which makes the headline
hard to compare. Single-crop evaluation is now the convention.
Left column: claims of the paper that later work confirmed. Right column: this deck’s reading of what happened next — the paper itself makes none of these predictions.
